# Mahāsudassana Sutta (DN 17 (PTS DN ii 169))

**ID:** DN 17 (PTS DN ii 169)  
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Mahāsudassana Sutta  
**PTS:** DN ii 169  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0102m.mul3.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0102m.mul3.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāsudassana Sutta* (DN 17) is the seventeenth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya*. It serves as an expansion of an episode from the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16): when Ānanda laments that the Buddha intends to pass into final nirvana in Kusinārā, characterizing it as a remote jungle township, the Buddha explains that the city was once the magnificent capital Kusāvatī ruled by the legendary wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) Mahāsudassana [Norman 1983; Piya Tan 2004; Nattier 2008]. Having the character of a *jātaka*, the discourse identifies King Mahāsudassana as a past life of the Buddha [Anālayo 2010; Norman 1983]. The sutta details the king's earthly splendour, including the seven jewels of a universal monarch—the wheel, elephant, horse, gem, woman, treasurer, and counsellor—explaining that his greatness stemmed from his practice of generosity (*dāna*), self-control (*dama*), and self-restraint (*saṃyama*) [Tambiah 1984; Norman 1983; Piya Tan 2004]. King Mahāsudassana subsequently renounces his palace and wealth to cultivate meditative practice, specifically the four divine abodes (*brahma-vihāra*) [Gaffney 2003].

 Modern scholars have also studied the text's lavish cosmic descriptions in relation to the origins of Pure Land depictions of Sukhāvatī [Goldstone 1978; Halkias 2013].

**Sources**

- [Norman 1983] K.R. Norman, Pali Literature (1983) — Discussion of the sutta as an expansion of DN 16, its jātaka character, and lay-oriented virtues.
- [Piya Tan 2004] Piya Tan, Maha Parinibbana Sutta (2004, 2008) — Context on the sutta's narrative link to Kusinārā and moral virtues of King Sudassana.
- [Tambiah 1984] Stanley Jeyaraja Tambiah, Buddhist Saints of the Forest and the Cult of Amulets (1984) — Listing of the seven jewels of the cakkavatti in the sutta.
- [Gaffney 2003] Sean D. Gaffney, Jātakanidānakathā: A critical study (2003) — Discussion of the four brahma-vihāras in the sutta.
- [Nattier 2008] Jan Nattier, Glorious Cities and Eminent Clans — Discussion of the Chinese parallel MĀ 68 and the setting of Kusinārā in DN 17.
- [Revire 2016] Nicolas Revire, Enthroned Buddha in Majesty: An Iconological Study (2016) — Rhys Davids' translation characterization and relation to the Sanskrit Mahāparinirvāṇa episode.
- [Radich 2011] Michael Radich, How Ajātaśatru Was Reformed (2011) — Inclusion of the Mahāsudassana episode in the mainstream Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra.
- [Anālayo 2010] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Genesis of the Bodhisattva Ideal (2010) — Comparison of DN 17 with the canonical Jātaka collection.
- [Goldstone 1978] Jane Nishi Goldstone, Eschatological Background of Devotionalism in Buddhist China (1978) — Comparison between King Sudassana's palace and Pure Land imagery.
- [Halkias 2013] Georgios T. Halkias, Luminous Bliss: Pure Land Literature in Tibet — Citation of scholarship on DN 17 and Sukhāvatī literature.
